items.title: Soybeans widen their lead over $11 per bushel
items.description: Afternoon Market Recap: Winter wheat prices faded into the red on Tuesday, with corn posting lightly mixed results.
items.summary:
Winter wheat prices plunged $1.23 per bushel on Monday, falling to $7.89. This represents a 13.5% drop in one day. The selloff was driven by expectations of a larger-than-expected U.S. winter wheat crop, which the USDA forecasts could reach 1.27 billion bushels, up 3% from 2022.

Soybean prices also trended lower, with March soybeans closing at $15.16 per bushel, down 10 cents. Meanwhile, March corn held onto fractional gains, closing at $6.74 per bushel.

Industry experts attribute the wheat price decline to the USDA's latest World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report, which projected higher domestic and global wheat supplies. This increased availability has weighed on prices, impacting farmers who had been hoping for stronger returns.

Looking ahead, the USDA will release its next WASDE report on February 8th. Farmers will be closely watching for any updates that could further influence wheat, corn, and soybean markets in the coming months.

items.title: The 2025 growing season in Illinois: good but not great
items.description: The 2025 growing season in Illinois delivered another storyline characterized by sharp weather contrasts, average crop condition ratings, some disease pressure in places, and very good — if not record-setting — yields in many, but not all, areas. As we have seen before, crops showed their ability to translate good mid-season conditions to good yields even with very dry late-season conditions. A tale of two springs March was 4-5 degrees warmer and 2-3 inches drier than normal statewide,…
items.summary:
Early spring was warmer and drier than normal, allowing for widespread early planting across most of the state. However, heavy rainfall in southern Illinois led to planting delays in that region.

Crops benefited from a warm and relatively dry June, with good root development and plant growth. Moderate drought developed in northern Illinois by late June, but July rainfall helped relieve it in many areas. Crop condition ratings improved to 65-70% good/excellent by the end of July.

However, the rainfall tap largely closed off in August, leading to worsening drought conditions through September, especially in central and southern Illinois. This dry late-season weather limited the crops' ability to complete grain fill, resulting in lower than expected final yields.

Key statistics:
- Corn yield: 214 bu/acre (3 bu less than 2024 record)
- Soybean yield: 62.5 bu/acre (1.5 bu less than 2024)
- Corn production: 2.35 billion bushels
- Soybean production: 639.3 million bushels

Factors contributing to the lower than expected yields included reduced kernel weights due to the dry August-September period, as well as some leaf disease pressure in parts of the state. Soybean seed size was also smaller than normal across trial sites.

Overall, the 2025 season demonstrated crops' ability to maintain productivity through early-season challenges, but the late-season drought stress ultimately limited yield potential in many fields. Farmers should continue to focus on soil moisture management and disease control strategies to prepare for variable growing conditions.

items.summary:
The American Sheep Industry Association (ASI) supports the timely reauthorization of a comprehensive five-year Farm Bill that emphasizes the need for long-term stability and benefits America's livestock producers. ASI President Ben Lehfeldt stated that a five-year Farm Bill provides the predictability and certainty that sheep producers need to make long-term business decisions. 

ASI appreciates the progress made in the previous One Big Beautiful Bill and looks forward to continuing those advancements in the 2026 Farm Bill. The sheep industry continues to face challenges from lamb imports, and ASI supports efforts to strengthen trade, conservation, research, and animal health provisions in the bill that benefit livestock agriculture.

Lehfeldt noted that livestock and sheep producers operate in a global marketplace facing volatile input costs, labor challenges, weather extremes, and trade uncertainty. A stable and forward-looking Farm Bill that addresses these issues will help ensure that producers can continue supplying high-quality American lamb and wool.

items.summary: The chief commodities economist with Stone X Group, Arlan Suderman, says the Trump administration's final biofuel blending requirements and a possible trade deal with China could significantly impact U.S. farmers' corn and soybean planting decisions. These factors are expected to come after the USDA has completed its planting intention surveys, and may not be reflected in the USDA's data. If China follows through on purchasing more U.S. agricultural products, it could shift some acres from soybeans to corn. Similarly, changes to biofuel blending requirements could also affect the relative demand for corn versus soybeans, leading farmers to adjust their planting plans accordingly. These policy decisions and trade dynamics, rather than the USDA's projections, may be the most important factors shaping the ultimate corn and soybean acreage in the U.S.

items.title: AgriLife Extension publishes human, pet fact sheets on New World screwworm
items.description: New resources expand education on potential risks The post AgriLife Extension publishes human, pet fact sheets on New World screwworm appeared first on AgriLife Today.
items.summary:
The Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service has released two new fact sheets on the New World screwworm, a potentially devastating parasite that can infest humans, pets, livestock, and wildlife. 

The key information includes:

- New World screwworm poses a significant threat, and infestations can be fatal if left untreated. 
- As of January 2026, the U.S. has reported 1 travel-related human case.
- Risk factors for humans include traveling to regions where screwworm is present, working closely with livestock/wildlife, and having open wounds.
- Pets near the southern U.S. border and those traveling to/from Latin America are at highest risk. Veterinary advice is recommended for pre-travel treatment.
- Early detection is essential for effective treatment of pets.
- Protection tips include daily pet checks, assessing the pet environment, and monitoring for unusual behavior.
- There are no confirmed cases in Texas yet, but Texans are encouraged to report any suspected cases to healthcare providers, the Texas Animal Health Commission, or Texas Parks and Wildlife Department.

The two new fact sheets, authored by AgriLife Extension experts, provide research-based information on risk factors, prevention, and reporting for both human health and companion animal care.

items.title: Economist says U.S. farmland values are outpacing rental income
items.description: A new study from Ohio State University indicates a shift is occurring in the farmland market.  Professor emeritus Carl Zulauf says U.S. land values have started to outpace the rise in rental rates. “After about 25-year period of fairly stable agricultural cropland, it began to suddenly increase,” he says. “We may be hitting a peak now, but […] The post Economist says U.S. farmland values are outpacing rental income appeared first on Brownfield Ag News.
items.summary:
Key points:

- A study from Ohio State University economist Carl Zulauf found that U.S. farmland values have started to increase faster than rental rates over the past 25 years.

- After a 25-year period of relatively stable agricultural cropland values, they have suddenly started increasing.

- Zulauf says farmland values may now be reaching a peak, but cautions that the trend of values outpacing rents could continue.

- This shift indicates a decoupling of farmland values from underlying rental incomes, which is an important consideration for farmers and landowners.

- The rapid rise in farmland values, if unchecked, could make it more difficult for young and beginning farmers to afford land purchases.

- Experts recommend that farmers and landowners closely monitor this trend and adjust their land acquisition and rental strategies accordingly.

items.title: Glyphosate Under Protection and Bayer’s Hope for Resolution
items.description: Executive order shields glyphosate supply as Supreme Court review and Bayer’s $7.25B fund reshape legal and food security outlook. The post Glyphosate Under Protection and Bayer’s Hope for Resolution appeared first on CropLife.
items.summary:
The U.S. government issued an executive order to protect the glyphosate supply, as the Supreme Court is set to review glyphosate-related lawsuits. Bayer has also established a $7.25 billion settlement fund to resolve future claims that glyphosate causes cancer. 

The executive order aims to ensure an adequate supply of glyphosate, a widely used herbicide, amid ongoing legal challenges. This comes as the Supreme Court considers reviewing lower court decisions that awarded billions in damages to plaintiffs who alleged glyphosate caused their cancer.

Bayer, which acquired Monsanto (the maker of glyphosate-based Roundup), has set aside $7.25 billion to resolve future lawsuits related to glyphosate. This settlement fund is part of Bayer's strategy to put the glyphosate litigation behind the company and provide more certainty for farmers who rely on the herbicide.

The protection of the glyphosate supply and Bayer's settlement fund are intended to maintain access to this key agricultural chemical and provide some resolution to the legal uncertainty surrounding glyphosate. This is important for farmers who depend on glyphosate for weed control and crop productivity.

items.title: Meat inspection: Following the gold standard
items.description: In an exclusive visit, the nation’s top food safety official stands behind the current U.S. meat inspection system.
items.summary: The U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Food Safety & Inspection Service (FSIS) Administrator Al Almanza stated that the current meat inspection system in the U.S. is the "gold standard" globally. Almanza emphasized that the U.S. meat inspection process is rigorous, with over 8,000 FSIS employees overseeing inspections at over 6,400 federally inspected facilities. In 2015, FSIS conducted over 8 million food safety tests, and the agency has zero tolerance for unsafe products, rejecting nearly 16,000 loads of meat and poultry. Despite calls for increased privatization of inspections, Almanza affirmed the USDA's commitment to maintaining a robust government-run inspection program to protect consumer safety. He noted that the U.S. system has led to a foodborne illness rate 60% lower than the historical average, and that the agency continuously works to improve processes, with new technology and increased training for inspectors. Almanza asserted that the current USDA inspection protocols are the global "gold standard" that other countries should emulate.

items.title: Glyphosate Policy, Legal Battles Heat Up
items.description: Executive action and Supreme Court review intensify glyphosate debate, as Bayer settlement and supply chain policies reshape industry outlook. The post Glyphosate Policy, Legal Battles Heat Up appeared first on CropLife.
items.summary:
The use and regulation of glyphosate, a widely used herbicide, has become a contentious issue with increasing legal battles and policy changes:

- The Biden administration is reviewing the Environmental Protection Agency's 2020 decision to reapprove glyphosate, potentially leading to new restrictions. This comes amid ongoing lawsuits against Bayer, which acquired Monsanto (the maker of glyphosate-based Roundup) in 2018, over Roundup's cancer risks.

- Bayer reached a $10.9 billion settlement in 2020 to resolve about 125,000 Roundup cancer claims, but additional lawsuits continue. Bayer set aside $4.5 billion to address potential future claims.

- Major food companies like General Mills and Cheerios are now requiring farmers to reduce glyphosate use, potentially impacting its application across millions of acres of farmland in the U.S.

- In 2022, the Supreme Court agreed to review the EPA's safety assessment of glyphosate, which could have significant implications for its future use and regulation.

- Experts warn that restrictions or bans on glyphosate could force farmers to adopt more costly and labor-intensive weed management practices, impacting crop yields and profitability.

- The ongoing legal and regulatory battles around glyphosate underscore the need for farmers to stay informed and adapt to evolving policies and market demands related to this widely used herbicide.

items.title: What happened to this $400 million in drought aid for farmers?
items.description: The $400 million was to be distributed through a financial institution that implements specific agricultural programs established by the federal government. The post What happened to this $400 million in drought aid for farmers? appeared first on AGDAILY.
items.summary:
In 2024, the USDA's Water-Saving Commodities program was set to provide up to $15 million each to 18 irrigation districts across 12 western states, as well as grants for 3 tribal communities and 2 state conservation district associations. This $400 million fund was intended to help farmers in drought-stricken areas upgrade aging irrigation infrastructure and more precisely regulate water levels.

The program had been finalized and grant recipients were notified by the end of 2024, with the expectation that payments would start flowing in 2025 over a 5-year period. However, since the change in administration, the funding has been frozen and grant recipients have received no communication or indication on whether the program will proceed.

Some key facts:
- The Central Arizona Irrigation and Drainage District was one of the selected recipients, planning to use the $15 million grant to replace deteriorating canal gates.
- Other recipients like the Palisade Irrigation District in Colorado and Hidalgo & Cameron Counties Irrigation District 9 in Texas have also heard nothing about the status of the program.
- The severe drought conditions in these regions have only worsened, forcing districts to dramatically cut back on irrigated acreage.
- Reasons for the funding freeze are unclear, with speculation it may be due to the program's climate change focus or simply a lack of remaining USDA staff after mass layoffs.

The article highlights the frustration and uncertainty felt by these drought-stricken farmers and irrigation districts, who were counting on this critical funding, and now have no idea if or when it will be released.

items.title: What happens now with IEEPA tariff revenue, new tariffs?
items.description: As farmers and agriculture leaders tried to figure out the impact of the Supreme Court ruling that President Trump does not have tariff power under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, the North Dakota Agricultural Trade Monitor...
items.summary:
Key Points:

- The U.S. government collected an estimated $958 million in tariff revenue on agricultural inputs between February and October 2025, including $273 million from chemicals, $530 million from farm machinery, $110 million from fertilizers, and $44 million from seeds.

- Following the Supreme Court ruling that President Trump does not have tariff power under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), this tariff revenue may have to be repaid, but it's unclear how and to whom.

- Over the weekend, President Trump imposed a new 15% global tariff that can last for 150 days. This means genuine relief for farmers is limited, as they will still face a 15% floor on input costs.

- The courts have reinforced that the power to place tariffs lies with Congress, with limited timeframes for the president. The administration may use other authorities to implement tariffs, and Congress will decide whether to extend or let the tariffs expire.

- The Supreme Court did not rule on requiring the payback of previous tariffs, which means farmers will not see immediate relief on lower input costs.

- The Trump administration plans to initiate investigations under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 on seafood, rice, and other products, and is committed to continuing its trade policy.

- USA Rice expressed disappointment with the Supreme Court decision.

items.title: Hard Water, Soft Control: How Carrier Quality Cuts Herbicide Performance
items.description: Hard water can slash herbicide performance; learn how pH, hardness, and fresh mixing protect burndown and residual results. The post Hard Water, Soft Control: How Carrier Quality Cuts Herbicide Performance appeared first on CropLife.
items.summary:
According to the article, hard water can significantly reduce the effectiveness of herbicides. Key points:

- Hard water, with high mineral content, can decrease the performance of burndown and residual herbicides by up to 50%. This is due to the minerals in the water interfering with the herbicide active ingredients.

- pH and water hardness are critical factors - ideal pH is 4-6, and hardness should be less than 300 ppm calcium carbonate. Levels outside this range can impair herbicide activity.

- Properly treating water by lowering pH and softening can improve herbicide efficacy by 10-20%. Using ammonium sulfate, acidifiers, or water conditioners can help achieve the ideal water conditions.

- Mixing herbicides with fresh, clean water immediately before application is recommended to prevent the water quality from degrading the product over time.

- Experts advise farmers to test their water source and adjust accordingly to optimize herbicide performance and weed control.

items.title: 1 dead, 3 injured after explosion at Perdue feed mill in N.C.
items.description: One worker was killed and three others were injured after an early morning explosion and fire tore through an eight-story grain tower at Perdue Feed Mill. The post 1 dead, 3 injured after explosion at Perdue feed mill in N.C. appeared first on AGDAILY.
items.summary:
One worker is dead, and three others were injured following an early morning explosion and fire over the weekend at the Perdue Feed Mill facility in Hertford County, North Carolina. The blast occurred inside an eight-story grain tower around 2:15 a.m. on Saturday. Multiple local and state agencies responded, including area volunteer fire departments, Hertford County EMS, North Carolina Emergency Management, and the Office of the State Fire Marshal. 

By Sunday morning, two workers were treated for non-life-threatening injuries, and a third person was airlifted to a regional medical facility with serious injuries. The fourth worker was initially unaccounted for, but Perdue Farms later confirmed that the missing associate had died. 

The cause of the explosion remains under investigation by the North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation. Hertford County officials described the response as a multi-day operation involving fire suppression, search efforts, structural stabilization, and coordinated recovery operations. They said the focus remained on supporting the family, protecting responders, and serving the Cofield community.

No further details about the deceased worker or the injured employees have been released. Perdue Farms expressed deep sadness over the loss and stated they are cooperating fully with local authorities as they investigate the incident. Updates will be provided as more information becomes available.

items.title: Should market data add a beef x dairy category?
items.description: Ag economist recommends updating sales data reporting to show the impact of BxD crossed cattle on the beef supply chain.
items.summary:
Ag economist Dr. Glynn Tonsor proposes this change, noting that BxD cattle now make up 25-30% of fed cattle supplies. 

Currently, BxD cattle are grouped into the standard beef or dairy categories, obscuring their unique market dynamics. Dr. Tonsor's analysis finds that BxD cattle have carcass weights 100-150 lbs heavier than purebred dairy cattle, but 50-100 lbs lighter than typical beef breeds. This affects beef supply and pricing.

items.title: How do we measure progress in an industry where perfection is impossible?
items.description: Many people want agriculture to be perfectly sustainable, perfectly efficient, and perfectly transparent. But it's an impossible challenge to achieve that. The post How do we measure progress in an industry where perfection is impossible? appeared first on AGDAILY.
items.summary:
Key points:

- There is no single "perfect" version of agriculture that can address all climate, economic, and animal welfare concerns to everyone's satisfaction. 

- Progress in agriculture is measured against historical trends, not an imaginary ideal. Metrics like increased productivity, reduced inputs, and improved animal health are signs of progress, even if perfection remains elusive.

- Productivity has increased significantly over time due to advances in technology, genetics, and management practices. For example, today's livestock producers have decreased greenhouse gas emissions per pound of meat or milk produced.

- Measuring progress is challenging because there is no universally accepted benchmark. Individual farms can track their own improvements, but the industry as a whole is often judged against unrealistic expectations of perfection.

- The author argues that while perfection may be impossible, continuous progress through adaptation is the real success story of agriculture, which has fed a growing population despite changing environmental, economic, and social pressures.

items.title: Avian flu outbreak threatens to reverse falling egg prices
items.description: Farm Progress America: Mike Pearson takes a look at how egg prices could face potential surge as Avian Flu returns to Pennsylvania.
items.summary:
Avian flu has returned to Pennsylvania, threatening to reverse the recent decline in egg prices. 

In December 2022, Pennsylvania detected its first case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in a commercial layer flock. This led to the depopulation of 1.8 million laying hens. 

Prior to this outbreak, egg prices had been falling, with the national average price for a dozen large eggs dropping from a high of $5.46 in August 2022 to $4.25 as of early December 2022, a 22% decline.

However, the Pennsylvania outbreak may drive prices back up. Experts estimate egg production could drop by 6-7% nationally over the next few months due to the loss of the 1.8 million hens. This could push wholesale egg prices up by 50-75 cents per dozen.

The USDA confirmed that 57.8 million birds have been affected by HPAI across the country since the current outbreak began in February 2022. This includes 44 million laying hens. The outbreak has led to the depopulation of flocks in 47 states.

Farmers are advised to review their biosecurity practices and remain vigilant for signs of HPAI in their flocks. Strict biosecurity measures are critical to preventing the spread of the virus.

The expansion project started about three years ago, and the completion date is yet to be determined. If approved, the construction would involve more than 200 workers over two years, and the expanded dairy would employ around 40 full-time employees. It would also be an additional buyer of crops from area farms, and those farms could utilize more manure for fertilizing their crops.

The public comment period for the environmental assessment worksheet (EAW) is open until March 12, 2026. The EAW reviewed potential impacts to air, local geology, soils, groundwater, surface water, and other environmental factors. Key findings include:
- The expansion will add five covered liquid manure storage basins, increasing storage capacity from 102 million gallons to 250 million gallons.
- Pumping from an off-site well will be limited to 226 million gallons per year at a rate not to exceed 1,000 gallons per minute, subject to restrictions based on the flow conditions of the Pomme de Terre River.
- West River Dairy will construct water storage basins to store a contingency water supply in case off-site well pumping is limited during low-flow periods.
- Clean stormwater will be collected and directed into the water storage basins, avoiding contact with manure or feed storage areas.

After the public comment period, the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency will review all comments and determine whether additional environmental review will be necessary. If no further review is needed, the project will proceed through the permitting process.

items.summary:
This is the most H5N1 cases in the country. 

To address the outbreak, Pennsylvania's governor is deploying additional state resources, including 6 extra staff and increased testing capacity. Since January, the state has performed 8,000 H5N1 tests. Over 100 state, federal, and university personnel have been mobilized to assist the response.

The impacted poultry flocks include 2 large commercial egg facilities with 2.6 million and 1.4 million birds each, as well as smaller pullet, meat bird, turkey, and duck farms. In total, Pennsylvania has lost over 14.3 million birds to H5N1 since the outbreak began 4 years ago, with half those losses occurring just this year.

The outbreak is also affecting the dairy industry, with 214 dairy farms in the surveillance zones required to undergo regular bulk tank testing. While H5N1 is not deadly to cattle, it can severely impact milk production. There have been no dairy herd cases this year, but 1,088 herds across 19 states have been affected since 2024.

To prevent further spread, the state is urging all poultry producers to immediately reinforce biosecurity measures like limiting access, using protective clothing, cleaning/disinfecting, and monitoring flocks closely. Sick or dead birds should be reported immediately.

Pennsylvania is the only state with a dedicated HPAI Recovery Fund, which has paid out nearly $16 million to 300 poultry businesses to offset losses and improve biosecurity. Over $50 million remains in the fund to support impacted producers.

items.title: How to Define Success Metrics for Your Ag Equipment GTM Campaign
items.description: Marketing campaigns rarely fail because of the creative missing the mark. They fail because they are measured against the wrong objective. Too often, performance is summarized in a single number: click-through rate. CTR is easy to report, easy to benchmark and easy to optimize toward. But easy does not mean effective. Clicks do not sell […] The post How to Define Success Metrics for Your Ag Equipment GTM Campaign appeared first on Farm Journal.
items.summary:
Key Takeaways:

- Marketing campaigns often fail because they are measured against the wrong objectives, with a common metric being click-through rate (CTR) which does not necessarily translate to equipment sales.

- OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) campaigns focused on brand-level marketing should measure metrics like reach, engagement, view-through conversions, and branded search lift, rather than just CTR.

- Dealer-focused campaigns should measure tangible results like phone calls, form submissions, test drive inquiries, and verified local buyer engagement, rather than just impressions or traffic.

- Optimizing for clicks can skew the audience toward high-frequency digital engagers rather than serious buyers, which is problematic in high-consideration categories like agricultural equipment.

- As farmer budgets tighten and dealer relationships face pressure, OEMs need to demonstrate brand value and support downstream sales, requiring disciplined alignment between objectives, audience strategy, and measurement framework.

- The solution is to define clear business objectives (OEM brand vs. dealer demand), select the appropriate audience strategy, and choose measurement metrics that validate attention and qualified intent, not just activity.

items.summary:
Brazil is increasing domestic potash production to reduce its reliance on imports, mainly from Canada and Russia. This could disrupt the global potash market and impact U.S. ag retailers.

Brazil produces only 10% of its potash needs, importing the remaining 90% mainly from Canada (44%) and Russia (22%). In 2021, Brazil imported 11.3 million metric tons of potash worth $3.6 billion. 

To boost domestic production, Brazil is investing $6.7 billion to develop new potash mines by 2025. This could increase Brazil's potash production from 0.4 million metric tons to 3 million metric tons annually.

The reduced reliance on imports could lead to lower potash prices in Brazil, potentially making Brazilian crops more competitive globally. This would impact U.S. ag retailers, who may face lower fertilizer prices and tighter margins.

Additionally, Brazil's efforts to diversify potash sources amid geopolitical tensions could create new supply chain risks and pricing volatility for U.S. ag retailers. Potential trade barriers or sanctions could disrupt the global potash market.

Experts recommend that U.S. ag retailers closely monitor Brazil's potash strategy and its impacts on the global market. They should also explore alternative risk management strategies to adapt to the changing landscape.

Key Summary:

The canvasback duck, once known as the "King of the Marsh", is under threat from habitat loss due to wetland drainage, pollution, and other factors. However, conservation efforts like Ohio's H2Ohio water quality initiative are helping to restore wetlands and protect the species.

- Canvasback ducks are large, fast-flying diving ducks that rely on aquatic plants like wild celery for food. They breed in the prairie pothole regions and migrate along the Mississippi and Pacific Flyways.

- Canvasbacks were once heavily hunted for the commercial market, nearly leading to their extinction, until the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918 banned market hunting.

- Today, habitat loss remains the main threat, with wetland drainage, water pollution, and loss of aquatic plants impacting their breeding and wintering grounds.

- Ohio's H2Ohio program, launched in 2019, is an ambitious water quality initiative that has funded over 499 wetland projects, restoring nearly 20,000 acres of wetlands. This helps create and enhance habitat for canvasbacks and other wildlife.

- H2Ohio works through partnerships with state agencies and conservation groups to implement best farming practices, reduce runoff, and revitalize water infrastructure - a collaborative effort to ensure the future of species like the canvasback.

- Experts emphasize that habitat conservation must be an ongoing effort, not just something done in the past, to protect migratory waterfowl like the canvasback.

items.title: Is sulfur a mobile nutrient? Carryover, soybean needs, and S fertilizer product differences
items.summary:
Key Takeaways:

- Sulfur can carry over in Minnesota soils for at least 2 years after application, providing enough sulfur for corn crops. Applying 10 lbs/acre of sulfate for 4 years resulted in carryover that covered corn's sulfur needs for 2 additional years.

- Soybeans do need sulfur, but direct sulfur application may not always benefit soybean yield. Sulfur applied for the preceding corn crop is usually sufficient for the following soybean crop.

- Elemental sulfur and sulfur-bentonite products like Tiger-Sul can be slower to become available than sulfate sources. Immediate incorporation of these products can reduce availability.

- Recommended practices:
  - Apply sulfur to high-demand crops like corn, alfalfa, and canola. Soybean may not need direct sulfur application.
  - Fall application of sulfate can be effective, as it can carry over to the next spring.
  - For elemental/bentonite products, avoid immediate incorporation after application to allow for better dispersal and oxidation.
  - Consider applying additional sulfate or thiosulfate for a few years when using elemental/bentonite products, until the previous sulfur applications become fully available.

The article was funded by the Agricultural Fertilizer Research and Education Council (AFREC) and the Minnesota Soybean Research and Promotion Council.

items.title: Improving waterhemp control by managing spray water pH
items.summary:
The study conducted in Rochester, Minnesota in 2025 evaluated how spray water pH adjustment and the timing of spray solution mixing affected waterhemp control in a corn herbicide program. The treatments included a tank mix of atrazine and Acuron GT (at full or half rate) with NIS and AMS, with or without a pH-lowering and buffering adjuvant (AlpHa Shot), and mixed either six days prior to application or at the time of spraying.

Adding the pH-lowering adjuvant reduced spray water pH from 7.5 to 5.8, which improved waterhemp control by 10% at 24 days after treatment (DAT) and 7% at 112 DAT. Waterhemp density decreased by 64% and biomass was reduced by 55% in treatments with the pH adjuster, resulting in lower late-season weed pressure and seed production potential.

The timing of mixing the pH adjuster (six days ahead or at time of spraying) did not affect waterhemp control, density, or biomass, which is important for applicators managing weather delays. The response to pH adjustment was observed at both full and half rates of Acuron GT, indicating that water quality can influence herbicide performance regardless of rate.

The key takeaway for applicators is that ensuring the spray water is conditioned to support herbicide performance is crucial, regardless of when the spray solution is mixed. Testing water pH and using a water conditioner or buffering agent can be a simple but impactful step to improve waterhemp control and season-long weed management.

items.title: 5 Cover Crops You Can Plant in February
items.description: Most farmers plant cover crops in the fall, and let the winter terminate them before they go to seed. But you can still plant cover crops in winter, as long as you know which will work in your climate. Plant these five cover crops this month for early spring benefits. The post 5 Cover Crops You Can Plant in February appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
Spinach: Spinach is an easy cold-season ground cover that increases good soil bacteria and fungi, especially beneficial for growing peppers later. It requires soil temperatures of at least 40°F (4°C) to germinate.

2. Kale: Kale cover crops feed the soil, farmers, and livestock. It requires slightly warmer soil of at least 45°F (7°C) to grow. Resistant varieties are recommended in areas with year-round diseases.

3. Daikon radish: Also called forage radishes, these have deep taproots that break up compacted soil and scavenge leftover nitrogen. They require soil temperatures of at least 65°F (18°C) to plant.

4. Oats: Oats grow quickly, cover soil, and form beneficial relationships with fungi. Planting a mix of oats and peas provides nitrogen-fixing benefits. Oats can tolerate temperatures down to 20°F (-7°C).

5. Buckwheat: Buckwheat is a quick-maturing cover crop that conditions poor soil and attracts pollinators. It can be used as a mulch after termination.

The article recommends sowing these cover crops at rates of 4-6 oz per 100 sq ft. Using low tunnels can help provide extra warmth and protection in colder climates. Planting spring crops after these cover crops can boost subsequent yields.

items.title: Frosting Seeding Legumes
items.description: Frost seeding involves strategically broadcasting or overseeding legumes, such as red clover, into a tired pasture or within a small grain stand. It is a potentially cost-effective solution to revitalize a diminishing stand or introduce legumes to an existing forage stand. Frost seeding is usually not recommended with grass species. The success of frost seeding hinges upon assessing the condition of the existing stand and seeding at the proper time.
items.summary:
Key Takeaways:

- Frost seeding involves strategically broadcasting or overseeding legumes like red clover into existing pastures or small grain stands to revitalize the stand. It is a cost-effective solution.

- Timing is critical - frost seeding is typically done between mid-February and early March to coincide with the freeze-thaw cycle, which helps incorporate the seed into the soil.

- The condition of the existing stand is important. A thick thatch can hinder seed-to-soil contact, so it's recommended to closely hay or over-graze the area beforehand.

- Soil type matters - frost seeding is more successful on loam or clay soils with enough moisture, as the freeze-thaw cycle is less effective on sandy or very dry soils.

- Adequate spring moisture is vital for establishing a healthy, frost-seeded stand. Timing, soil condition, and moisture are key factors in the success of frost seeding.

- The article was written by Dr. Shelby Gruss, an assistant professor and forage extension specialist who joined Iowa State University in November 2023. Her research focuses on optimizing forage-based systems.

items.summary:

items.title: Why Attention Matters More Than Response for Advertisers
items.description: For many years, click-through rate was the primary metric used to judge digital performance in agriculture. Today, it no longer tells the full story. Farmers are searching differently, using AI-assisted tools, voice search and quick-scan platforms that often answer their questions without the need to click at all. With this shift, the true indicator of […] The post Why Attention Matters More Than Response for Advertisers appeared first on Farm Journal.
items.summary:
Farmers are now using AI-assisted tools, voice search, and quick-scan platforms that often provide answers without requiring a click. 

The true indicator of content effectiveness is now attention time - how long a user spends meaningfully engaged. A redesign of AgWeb.com demonstrates how increasing user attention and engagement can benefit advertisers:
- 54% increase in readers reaching 75% of an article 
- 21% increase in readers reaching 90% of an article
- 33% increase in daily article pageviews per mobile user

The article notes that only about 16% of users read content word-for-word, while 79% scan pages. Deeper engagement and more articles viewed per visit create more opportunities for meaningful brand impressions.

Attention time is a better indicator than click-through rate, as it shows if users stayed with the content, scrolled with purpose, and consumed multiple articles. This directly influences brand recall, message retention, and advertising effectiveness.

The AgWeb redesign provides a template for increasing farmer engagement and attention. This benefits advertisers by placing their message in focused, engaged moments rather than fleeting impressions. The article concludes that better attention leads to better outcomes for ag marketers.

items.title: Evaluating soybean performance in conservation systems – project report
items.description: You can also read the article in Portuguese and Spanish Introduction Recent dust storm events in central Illinois and across the Midwest have renewed attention on soil conservation, especially after the tragic May 2023 event near Springfield that caused an 80-vehicle pileup, eight fatalities, and dozens of injuries. These incidents highlight that soil loss is not only an agronomic issue but also a public safety and environmental concern. Reduced tillage and cover crops are well-established pract
items.summary:
Starter fertilizer strategies tested were an unfertilized control, 15 lb N/acre, and 15 lb N/acre + 10 lb S/acre. 

Early-season soybean biomass and leaf nutrient status showed a positive response to starter fertilizer, but these differences did not persist to yield. Soybean yields ranged from 60-95 bu/acre across locations, with no significant yield differences between tillage/cover crop systems.

When accounting for operational costs, the NT system returned the highest partial net profit, followed by ST and CT. The NT+CR system had the lowest partial net return due to higher cover crop management costs, though these costs can be offset by government programs.

The study will continue in 2026 to track longer-term impacts on soils, residues, and nutrient dynamics under the conservation systems. Preliminary results indicate soybeans can maintain productivity under reduced tillage and cover crops without a yield penalty.

items.title: Forest Farming: Why it Might Make Sense for Your Land
items.description: Also called agroforestry, forest farming is a great way to work within your environmental parameters and utilize the tree canopy to produce more for your farm. Especially for those who live in forested areas, this practice enhances farm output without compromising the ecosystem. The post Forest Farming: Why it Might Make Sense for Your Land appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
Main findings:
- Forest farming, also known as multi-story cropping or agroforestry, is the practice of integrating small-scale farming with conventional forestry. This results in a self-sustaining system that works within local ecological bounds.
- The most common form involves thinning a forest to allow the best conditions for crops to grow in the understory, such as native ornamentals, fungi, fruit, timber, and forest food crops.
- Forest farming brings benefits like improved water and soil quality, carbon storage, and diversified crop options. It's suitable for farms with existing forest land or areas near riparian zones.

Key details:
- Originates in Brazil's tropical rainforests, where it is a necessity due to high biodiversity and productivity.
- Can be implemented on small farms with just a bit of forest land.
- Requires inventory of natural resources, development of a forest management plan, and alignment with local market demands.
- Regulations may apply to wild plant species, especially those under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES).

Impacts for farmers:
- Provides an opportunity to diversify farm products and tap into specialty crop markets.
- Improves ecological benefits like water quality, carbon sequestration, and biodiversity.
- Can be a relatively low-cost way to integrate forestry and farming.

Recommendations/action items:
- Consult local agricultural extension, state forestry agencies, and trusted market contacts to plan and implement a forest farming system.
- Carefully consider which trees and crops are best suited to your land and local conditions.
- Be proactive about marketing and selling forest-grown products through various channels.

items.title: Purdue researchers adopt interdisciplinary approach to assessing emerging tar spot disease in corn
items.description: For more than a century, tar spot fungal disease in corn kept its distance from the U.S., biding its time
items.summary:
Purdue researchers are taking an interdisciplinary approach to assess the emerging tar spot disease in corn:

- Tar spot, a fungal disease in corn, was not detected in the U.S. prior to 2015 but has since spread to 16 states and Ontario, Canada.

- Researchers led by C.D. Cruz, associate professor at Purdue, are using a mix of statistical analysis, data science, epidemiology, microbiology, AI, and computer vision to understand the dynamics of tar spot.

- Their work is funded by two USDA grants totaling nearly $1.1 million.

- Collaborators include researchers from Colombia, Mexico, Ecuador, South Korea, and the U.S.

- Previous efforts include developing a digital method to quantify tar spot in corn, which was published in 2021. Ongoing efforts are refining the model's accuracy.

- Researchers from the civil engineering department are also involved, adapting their AI and computer vision approaches to inspect and analyze crop disease.

- A current project aims to integrate drone imagery and weather data to build a model that can detect and track tar spot progress, correlating with human disease evaluations.

- The interdisciplinary nature of the project can be challenging, but it leads to better problem-solving by bringing diverse expertise to the table.

- The researchers' goal is to quantify and model tar spot severity to provide rapid and accurate information to stakeholders and address this emerging biosecurity threat.

Farmers are advised to monitor their fields closely and be prepared to apply fungicides if needed. Damon Smith, Extension Field Crops Pathologist, recommends applying fungicides at Feekes growth stage 8 or 9 to protect the flag leaf, the most important leaf for yield.

items.title: Questions to consider prior to replanting a soybean field
items.description: Shawn P. Conley, Soybean and Small Grains Specialist, UW-Madison Early in the growing season, abiotic (freezing temperatures, hail, flooding, etc.) and biotic (slugs, deer, disease, insects, etc.) factors often reduce soybean plant stands. A soybean …
items.summary:
Key points include:

Factors that can reduce soybean plant stands early in the season include abiotic stresses (freezing temperatures, hail, flooding) and biotic stresses (slugs, deer, disease, insects).

If plant stands are reduced below 100,000 plants/acre, farmers should consider replanting. Replanting is typically recommended if stands are below 75,000 plants/acre.

Factors to consider when deciding to replant include potential yield loss, planting date, and replanting costs. Replanting later in the season can result in yield losses of 0.5-1 bu/acre per day.

Replanting costs can range from $30-$50/acre, including seed, fuel, and labor. Farmers should carefully weigh the potential yield increase from replanting versus the replanting costs.

Shawn P. Conley, Soybean and Small Grains Specialist at UW-Madison, advises farmers to carefully inspect fields and do stand counts before making a replanting decision.

items.title: Spraying 2,4-D on Soybean in 2024?
items.description: Daniel H. Smith, Outreach Program Manager, UW-Madison Division of Extension, Rodrigo Werle, Weed Scientist and Extension Specialist, UW-Madison Are you planning to spray 2,4-D for postemergence broadleaf weed control in Enlist E3 soybean? The 2,4-D …
items.summary:
The UW-Madison article discusses the use of 2,4-D herbicide for weed control in Enlist E3 soybean crops.

Key points:
- 2,4-D will be labeled for postemergence broadleaf weed control in Enlist E3 soybeans starting in 2024.
- Farmers need to be aware of 2,4-D use restrictions, including application timing, nozzle selection, drift management, and buffer requirements.
- Applying 2,4-D too late in the soybean growth stage can lead to crop injury. The recommended application window is from soybean emergence to the R1 (beginning bloom) stage.
- Proper nozzle selection and sprayer setup are critical to minimize off-target movement of 2,4-D. Coarse or ultra-coarse droplets are recommended.
- Buffers of at least 240 feet are required when applying 2,4-D near sensitive crops like grapes, tomatoes, and fruit trees.
- Careful planning and communication with neighbors are essential to avoid unintended crop damage from 2,4-D drift.

Experts quoted:
- Daniel H. Smith, Outreach Program Manager, UW-Madison Division of Extension
